podcast.title: Guitarist Wes Borland's Departures and Return (2001-2004)
podcast.body: Guitarist Wes Borland initially quit the band in 2001. He was replaced by Mike Smith, but Smith departed by 2004, leading to Borland's return. "First guitarist Wes Borland had quit 2001. He was replaced by Mike Smith, but by 2004 he had gone. Wes was back."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakup Date (November 8, 2005)
podcast.body: This date, following the release of their greatest hits album and subsequent silence, is used as the band's official breakup date. "So what we're going to do is use that date as our breakup date. November 8th 2005."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Public Disfavor & Internal Issues (Mid-2005)
podcast.body: By mid-2005, Limp Biscuit, and Fred Durst in particular, had "worn out their welcome with the public" as their sound and approach had gone "out of style." This period was also marked by internal problems. "But by the middle of 2005, Limp Biscuit in general and Fred Durst in particular had worn out their welcome with the public."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reunion Rumors (Fall 2008)
podcast.body: By the fall of 2008, rumors began circulating that the band's internal differences had been resolved and they were reuniting. "There were rumors that differences had been fixed and that Limp Biscuit was back together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Reunion Gig (May 2009) – Riga, Latvia
podcast.body: Three months after the reunion announcement, the original lineup, which had not been seen together in eight years, played their first gig in Riga, Latvia. "Three months later, the original lineup, something that we hadn't seen in eight years played their first gig together."

podcast.title: New Album Work Begins (August 24, 2009)
podcast.body: By August 24, 2009, all members of the reunited band had begun working on a new album. "And in August the 24th of 2009, everyone started working on a new album."

podcast.title: Reunion Announcement (February 11, 2009)
podcast.body: On this date, Fred Durst posted a message on Twitter – "1am Pacific time. Limp Biscuit.com tonight" – signaling the band's official return. "And on February 11th of 2009, those who were following Fred on Twitter... got this message. 1am Pacific time. Limp Biscuit.com tonight."

podcast.title: Fred Durst as Executive
podcast.body: Executives at the band's record company thought highly enough of Fred Durst to appoint him an executive. "executives at their record company thought enough of Fred Durst to make him an executive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rapid Decline
podcast.body: The band experienced a swift decline at the end of the 90s due to "ill-advised career moves," including their controversial Woodstock 99 appearance, and the release of "below-par albums." "they flamed up pretty fast at the end of the 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Symbol of New Metal's Downfall
podcast.body: Limp Biscuit came to symbolize "the worst of new metal" and became the central focus of the backlash against the genre, despite attracting 50,000 people to stadium shows. "If it's just one band that came to symbolize the worst of new metal and a group that was the focus of the backlash, it was Limp Biscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Time Apart (3 years, 3 months, 3 days)
podcast.body: The band was apart for this duration, from their designated breakup date of November 8, 2005, to their reunion announcement on February 11, 2009. "Let Biscuit and Nookie, apart for three years, three months and three days."

concerts.body: The band's appearance at Woodstock 99 was marred by violence and destruction, contributing to their "ill-advised career moves" and backlash. "an appearance at Woodstock 99 that was marred by violence and destruction."

xref.title: 2000 Sales Performance
xref.body: The band sold 4 million records in the year 2000, making them one of the few successful New Metal acts during a time when rock music was struggling. "Limp Biscuit sold 4 million records in 2000."

xref.title: Confrontation with Fred Durst (Summer 2000)
xref.body: A concert in New York that summer saw Fred Durst of Limp Biscuit diss singer Scott Stapp, to which Stapp responded by challenging Durst to a boxing match. "Actually, the end of Creed involved a fight with Limp Biscuit. There was a concert in New York that summer, and Fred Durst discreed singer Scott Stapp, and Stapp responded by challenging Fred to a boxing match."

xref.title: Public Backlash (Mid-2000)
xref.body: Similar to Limp Biscuit, Creed quickly experienced a public backlash beginning sometime in mid-2000. "And like Limp Biscuit, they saw the public turn on them rather quickly, beginning sometime in mid 2000."

xref.title: Contribution to Nu-Metal
xref.body: Despite controversies, Body Count persevered and played a significant role in the emergence of the nu-metal movement during the mid to late 1990s, influencing bands like KoRn, Slipknot, and Limp Bizkit. "But the band continued, and they were a big part of the move into new metal in the middle in late 90s. So basically, you can draw a line from Body Count, right through corn, slipknot, and limp biscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Discovery by Korn's Fieldy
xref.body: After Korn's encounter with Fred Durst, Durst strategically sent a Limp Bizkit demo tape to Fieldy, a member of Korn. Fieldy was impressed by the demo and subsequently passed it on to Korn's management and the emerging nu-metal producer Ross Robinson. This crucial step paved the way for Limp Bizkit's major label deal. "When Corn got home, Fieldy found a limp biscuit demo in his mailbox."

xref.title: Estate as Zero DB Initiative Signatory
xref.body: The estate of Prince is among the signatories of the Zero DB initiative, formed in 2008 by the charity Reprieve. This initiative encourages condemnation of music as torture and advocates for governments to enforce the Convention Against Torture and other treaties concerning prisoner treatment. "The Sinees include Tom Morello, average against the machine, members of REM, rise against Pearl Jam, Trent Reznor, Limp Biscuit, system of a down, disturbed the estate of Prince, the Chili Peppers, Eminem, Marilyn Manson, Neil Diamond, Dr. Dre, and a host of others."

xref.title: Influence from Body Count
xref.body: Slipknot is part of the lineage of bands influenced by Body Count, connecting them to the origins of the nu-metal movement. "So basically, you can draw a line from Body Count, right through corn, slipknot, and limp biscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Major Label Deal and Rise to Prominence
xref.body: Following the positive reception of their demo by Korn's Fieldy and producer Ross Robinson, Limp Bizkit quickly secured a major label deal. This set them on a path to become one of the most successful and impactful bands of the nu-metal era, known for their aggressive and in-your-face style. "And before long, limp biscuit had a major label deal and were on their way to becoming one of the most successful and most in-your-face bands of the new metal era."
